title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Medication Dosage Calculations & Safe Math
html:
Medication calculation is a clinical-safety process, not an isolated arithmetic exercise. The RN verifies the order, client, allergies, relevant assessment data, available concentration, route, timing, and safe-dose parameters before calculating. A correct equation cannot make an incomplete, ambiguous, or inappropriate order safe.

Learning goals

  • Convert common metric and weight units accurately.
  • Use dimensional analysis or the desired-over-have formula while keeping units visible.
  • Calculate tablet, liquid, injectable, weight-based, divided, and basic infusion doses.
  • Compare a calculated dose with the ordered safe range.
  • Apply safe decimal notation and sensible rounding.
  • Pause and clarify when the order, label, result, or dose range does not make sense.

Begin with a safety screen

Read the complete order and medication label. Identify the dose ordered, the dose or concentration available, the quantity that contains the available dose, and the unit requested in the answer. Confirm whether a weight-based order is written per dose or per day. Use the most current measured weight required by the order and verify whether it is recorded in kilograms. Review client-specific data and medication parameters before preparing the dose.

Math does not authorize administration
If an order is unclear, the label does not match, the calculated amount is impractical, or the dose falls outside an ordered or referenced safe range, stop and clarify through the approved process. Never alter the order to create a convenient answer.

Keep the units visible

Dimensional analysis places conversion factors so unwanted units cancel and the requested unit remains. The desired-over-have formula expresses the same relationship: desired dose ÷ dose on hand × quantity on hand = amount to give. Before accepting an answer, confirm that the remaining unit is the unit you need—tablets, mL, or mL/hr—and estimate whether the result is reasonable.

Core conversions

  • 1 kg = 2.2 lb
  • 1 g = 1,000 mg
  • 1 mg = 1,000 mcg
  • 1 L = 1,000 mL
  • 60 minutes = 1 hour

Convert to matching units before applying the formula. For pounds to kilograms, divide pounds by 2.2. Avoid mixing household and metric measures when a metric dosing device is available.

Tablets, liquids, and injections

For tablets, determine how many tablets contain the ordered dose. Split only a formulation designed and approved to be split, and follow pharmacy and organizational guidance. For liquids and injections, read concentration as a relationship such as 250 mg in 5 mL or 2 mg/mL. Select a device that can measure the calculated volume accurately; small oral volumes generally require an appropriately sized oral syringe rather than a household spoon.

Weight-based and divided doses

First convert weight to kilograms when needed, then calculate carefully from the exact order. mg/kg/dose gives the amount for each dose. mg/kg/day gives the total amount for 24 hours and must be divided by the ordered number of doses when the order calls for divided dosing. Do not confuse every-8-hours with eight doses per day: every 8 hours is three doses in 24 hours.

Safe-dose range is a separate check

Calculate the minimum and maximum safe dose using the client’s weight and the stated reference range. Then compare the ordered dose with that interval. Being able to calculate a volume does not prove the dose is appropriate. If it is outside the range—or if the reference, indication, formulation, or order is uncertain—hold preparation or administration as appropriate and clarify with the prescriber and pharmacist according to policy.

Basic infusion rates

For a pump rate, total volume in mL ÷ time in hours = mL/hr. Convert minutes to hours when necessary. Recheck the total volume, duration, concentration, route, line, pump settings, and ordered limits. High-alert medication calculations and pump programming may require an independent double-check under organizational policy.

Round only at the end

Carry the calculation without premature rounding, then round the final answer according to the medication, measuring device, pharmacy preparation, and organizational policy. A mathematically rounded amount is unsafe if the device cannot measure it accurately. Always include the unit with the answer.

Write decimals safely

Use a leading zero for an amount less than one: 0.5 mg, not .5 mg. Do not use a trailing zero after a whole number: 5 mg, not 5.0 mg. These conventions reduce tenfold misreading risk. Write unit names and approved abbreviations clearly; never let a calculator display replace a complete medication check.

Worked examples

Liquid: Order 375 mg; available 250 mg/5 mL. Set up 375 mg × 5 mL ÷ 250 mg = 7.5 mL.

Weight-based divided dose: Order 30 mg/kg/day in three equal doses for a 15-kg client. Daily dose = 30 × 15 = 450 mg/day. Per dose = 450 ÷ 3 = 150 mg/dose.

Infusion: 1,000 mL over 8 hours. Rate = 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125 mL/hr.

Evaluate before and after administration

Before administration, repeat the rights and required checks, compare the prepared amount with the order and label, and resolve discrepancies. After administration, document according to policy and assess the intended response, adverse effects, and relevant clinical parameters. Report and respond to unexpected outcomes promptly.
